claim: When a person's report contradicts a green metric, reproduce the fault as the person meets it (input aimed away from the target, buttons held, the shipped build) before writing a cure, and accept the cure only on that same reproduction, because a stand-in that always aims at the target measures the rule it was built around, not the game the person plays.
because: A night of scripted play measured loose pucks taken 99.6 %; the person said the puck in his ring was still not his. Reproduced with the stick aimed 90 or 180 degrees away: 21 of 27 cases not his within 2 frames; after the cure 0 of 27, and through the person-like input path the win rate rose 92 to 98 % at the low level and 55 to 73 % at the middle one.

claim: When a person's play notes arrive, confirm from the machine's own start record which build they actually started before acting on them, and show the build's name on the first screen, because notes taken on an older build send every fix after a fault that is already gone.
because: The operating system's start record showed the last build started by hand was five packages older than the one the notes named, started four minutes before the notes; one of the two reported faults existed only in that older build. A launcher that always starts the newest package and a build tag on the first screen landed.

claim: When every figure in a release report was produced by scripted hands, say so in the report line until a person has played that build, because a reader takes a clean percentage for a statement about players.
because: The final play sheet states that all hardening, acceptance and filming was done by scripted hands and that nobody had played the last eight packages with a mouse; the habit followed two evenings on which green scripted figures were contradicted by the person.

claim: When a difficulty ladder's win rates are quoted, name the instrument that produced them, and when the instrument changes, report the old and new instrument side by side on the same commit instead of re-setting the ladder on the new one, because a change to the scripted player alone moves the cells by several points.
because: Fixing the scripted player's check press (misses 54 % to 16 %) moved the three cells from 87.2 / 52.8 / 28.2 to 84.8 / 56.3 / 31.5 on 600 paired seeds with no change to the game; the ladder was kept where the person had accepted it and both columns were reported.

claim: When a difficulty ladder is set for a person, measure it through the person's own input path (the real button resolver, tap and hold thresholds, a person-like hand), prove that path equal to the game to the hash, and locate the gap to the decision-level instrument by switching one component off at a time, because the two instruments disagree by double-digit points and the cause is usually the hand, not the buttons.
because: The input-path instrument matched the game to the hash at 12 of 12 checkpoints; the middle level read 31 % through injected decisions and 17.7 % through the input path; switched one at a time, buttons off gave 12 %, the person-like hand off 34 %. Two later ladder sets were made through that path (middle level 71.0 to 55.2 % at 600 seeds).

claim: When a difficulty curve is tuned, make the game's central skill a drill that gates every curve number (a pass rate from a fixed distance and a fail rate for the naive move), and ship a level off its target rather than buy the target with the skill's window, because the skill's window is what a person tests first.
because: The drill (a stop begun at 8 m beats a charging defender at least 80 %, a straight charge under 20 %) caught a combined change that broke it; one level shipped 4.4 points over its bar because the only lever that fixed the bar took the stop from 9.5 m from 97 % to 80.5 %; a wider hunt radius took the stop at 8 m to 24 %.

claim: When a rule change lands in a deterministic simulation, give it a data key with a neutral value that replays the previous game to the hash, prove the replay, and make every pinned-hash test read one shared baseline of neutral values, because a rule with a proven neutral can ship switched on, and pins kept per change stop each other.
because: Each rule of the last days shipped with a neutral proven to the hash (6 of 6 cells; 50 of 50 seeds a rink); before a shared baseline helper existed, five landings in one night stopped on each other's pinned hashes.

claim: When a game ships modes as rule data, measure each mode's difference from the base game and fuzz the mode data with every found case kept as a regression, because modes drift into copies of the base game and live changes carry values outside their declared ranges.
because: A soak found three modes no longer differing from the base game by a third, two season matches playing identically and a mode running past its own horn; a fuzz pass found seven fault classes, kept as regression data, and a hook value outside its parameter's range, now refused.

claim: When a carried ball or puck can be lost, let it leave the carrier only by an action (a shot, a pass, a poke, a lift, a hit that loosens it, the carrier's own release), never by an unpressed touch of a stick or a body, because a carry the field takes by contact lasts under a second and the game cannot be played around it.
because: The controlled player's carry lasted a median 0.87 / 0.75 / 0.67 s at three levels before the rule; with it his win rates moved from 85 / 48 / 26 targets to 99.8 / 72.0 / 39.8 and the ladder was re-set on the new game.

claim: When a person controls one figure, give a loose ball inside a drawn ring under that figure, or one its body moves through, to that figure on that frame whatever its aim points at, because a person's aim is elsewhere and a pickup by aim reads as the ball passing through the body.
because: With the aim held 90 or 180 degrees away, 21 of 27 cases were not his within 2 frames before and 0 of 27 after; the central skill drill was identical to the digit with the ring off and on; a 144-match escape scan grew no class.

claim: When a pickup ring serves the controlled figure, keep the figure's own release from it while the release is still leaving it, and only inside the ring, because the ring re-took a tapped pass one frame after release, and a lock applied everywhere slowed a pass to a mate.
because: A tapped pass was retaken one frame after release until the first 8 frames were kept and a 6 m/s margin applied; the first version freed the release everywhere and a carry assist pulled a pass back (26 vs 19 frames to the mate); after the fix 19 / 18 frames, equal to the neutral.

claim: When several rules test whether a figure carries the ball (shoot, pass, charge, carry), compute the carrier's reach once and use it in every test and in the opponents' logic, because a ball carried 1.6 m out against a shot test at 1.5 m let nothing fire while the player aimed.
because: Six packages in a row could not shoot or pass while aiming; with one reach used everywhere, 30 shots fired at three charge levels where the earlier read-out had none, and the input-driven acceptance run went 17 of 18 green.

claim: When a figure gets up from a knockdown or has just won the ball, give it a grace against a second knockdown or a stick take and choose the length from a run that counts repeat events, because a short grace still lets a figure be knocked down again moments after it rises.
because: A play-through found the controlled figure down every 7 s, 7 of 15 within a second of release; a 90-frame grace still allowed one repeat at 111 frames, a 120-frame grace allowed none in 1,000 s, and every difficulty cell stayed within 1 point.

claim: When possession changes while a button is held, ignore the held button until it is released and pressed again, and let a held charge die with the possession, because a press carried across a turnover fires a verb the person did not choose.
because: The rule landed in input and in the simulation (a held charge dies on loss); no difficulty cell moved more than 2.2 points and the opponents' goals by 0.06 a match at most.

claim: When a contact happens between figures, let the figures' own motion carry the whole event and draw nothing of the mechanics on or in front of them (no bar, arc, ring, plate or streak), because a mark meant as feedback reads to a person as a bug in the animation.
because: The person described a team-coloured bar at a cross-check as a technical rectangle instead of an animation; nine layers of marks were still drawn in the newest build; all were switched off with tests that pin their absence, and the walk of the cooked candidate found three more, cured with before and after films.

claim: When you must know what a person sees at a contact, film every simulation frame of the packaged build from the play camera at the shipped looks and sizes and read the frames, instead of counting switches or sampling the development binary, because counting and sampling called the marks gone while the film found them.
because: A count of 42 hit strips taken on the development binary reported no marks; filming every frame of the package found nine drawn layers, and a later walk of the cooked candidate found three more drawn at contacts.

claim: When a figure throws a hit, keep its own hit animation playing through contact and follow-through, and do not send it a collision reaction for the contact its own hit made, because the reaction one frame after contact replaced the take and none of it was drawn.
because: Frame by frame: press at frame 1338, collision reaction at 1339, not one frame of the cross-check take drawn; with four frames of air the arms dropped two frames before contact. A guard with its own test landed; knockdowns caused by a hit still play.

claim: When a fix is presentation only, prove it on the same simulation frames of the same binary, before and after side by side, with the simulation's hashes equal line by line, because that shows the fix changed what is seen and nothing that is played.
because: Every before and after film pair of the hit-mark removal carried equal simulation hashes line by line; the pairing and hash comparison tools were kept for the next lane.

claim: When a hit must read at play distance, lengthen the opponents' wind-up for the eye, keep the person's own press short, and measure the wind-up's cost on the difficulty ladder, because a longer wind-up is a cue to see, not a mechanic.
because: Opponent wind-ups of 8 and 12 frames against the person's 4 and 4: on 600 paired seeds the cost was -0.3 / +5.8 / +4.0 points for the body check and 0 for the cross-check; the person's knockdowns fell from 7.4 to 6.3 a match; a scripted dodge of a hit seen coming was worth nothing.

claim: When a build is packaged for a person, gate it on an acceptance run that plays its first minutes through the real cursor and buttons, verb by verb, and prove every new row of that run in a window before it joins the release chain, because tests that inject decisions pass builds a person cannot play.
because: Six packages shipped in which the player could not shoot or pass while aiming; the first input-driven acceptance run failed that build on shooting, passing and the one-timer and went 17 of 18 green on the fix; later, two releases failed on rows never run in a window.

claim: When a change is pushed, compile the shipping configuration first, not only in the release chain, because a test written outside its automation guard passes every gate and then stops the release at its first step.
because: Twice a test outside its guard passed every gate and stopped a release at the shipping compile; the landing chain gained the step and every later change reports a shipping pass.

claim: When off-screen QA starts the engine many times, run few processes with many seeds each, skip the per-start platform validation, and disable the asynchronous compute queue for off-screen QA runs only, because each start otherwise queues minutes on a build lock and the development binary crashes in its first frames off screen.
because: A three-match run went from 5 m 17 s to 9.5 s and the gate's test step from 398 s to 89 s with identical hashes; off-screen development starts crashed 9 of 30 times with the queue on, while 60 development and 20 shipping package starts did not; the shipped renderer settings were left alone.

claim: When a simulation is hardened before a release, report each run's size beside its result, run each soak twice in separate processes and compare per seed, and run a neutral arm showing the rule under test acted in those runs, because a clean result over runs where the new rule never fired proves nothing.
because: The final hardening reported 2,400 escape-scan matches, 600 fuzz matches played twice with equal hashes, 44 lockstep matches with loss and jitter and no desync, a neutral arm whose 12 of 12 matches differed from the rule-on run, 10,700 soak matches with no fault and 46 of 46 cells bit-identical on a second run, plus a list of what did not fit.

claim: When a gate prints a pass, compare the count of tests it completed with the count it found and with the previous run's count, and fail a run that was stopped or cut short, because a stopped run that counts only what passed reads as green.
because: A landing was reported green on 214 of 373 tests after a free-disk floor stopped the test run; a package was cut from that commit; the gate now fails an incomplete run and the full filter re-ran 373 of 373.

claim: When a game is submitted with a page, a form, a readme and a video, read every claim in them against the build as it will be submitted, give each a verdict (true; false now and rewritten; cannot be checked by reading, with what would check it; the owner's to answer), and re-run the table on every new candidate, because the game moves under its page.
because: One pass found 53 of 154 claims false against the candidate and rewrote them (75 true, 23 not checkable by reading, 3 for the owner); the next candidate's pass found 18 of 50 changed claims false.

claim: When a game's credits and a submission form name the tools and sources used, derive both from one generated-content ledger (one row per shipped or tried asset, with origin, tool and licence) and check the ledger against the package, because hand-written credits drift from what ships.
because: Regenerated from the ledger (2,281 rows), the credits showed that the credits screen named a generator with no shipped row while 41 rows of another shipped, and that the ledger called a library shipped which two packages lacked; the screen was corrected.

claim: When a director runs parallel agent lanes, give each lane a brief, a status file written from its first minute, explicit ready and source-open lines, and take a lane's tree only at a ready line with no source-open line after it, because the director's own process restarts and a tree taken mid-edit lands half-saved work.
because: The director's process restarted three times in two days and resumed from lane status files; two exports caught half-saved edits before the ready-line rule, none after.

claim: When a brief or a director states a premise or a cause, write it as a reading the lane is to prove or refute and tell the lane its measurement outranks the brief, because the director's stated cause of a red gate was wrong and the lane's measurement found the real one.
because: The director ruled that a shove from behind broke a skill drill; the lane measured 6,000 carries with no shove from behind and found the opponents going round the shield at any speed; the cure for the measured cause landed.

claim: When two machines share work through one remote, make the landing step refuse to run off its branch and read the remote back after every push, and cross the ownership line only by one request file per ask with a status line, an acceptance check and a deadline, because a push from a detached checkout prints success and sends nothing new.
because: The main checkout sat detached for six and a half hours; every landing printed pushed while the remote stayed put and the second machine received nothing; the branch check and the remote read-back were added to the landing step.

claim: When several rule or logic changes each pass their gate alone, land them together through one integration lane that owns the seam and rehearse the combined landing with the full gate in a scratch tree, because changes that each pass can fail together.
because: A logic change and a contact rule each passed alone and together broke the central skill drill (50 % against a bar of 80 %); both were parked and landed through an integration lane that measured and fixed the real cause.

claim: When landings and releases share one checkout, run one at a time under a lock that queued work waits on, never on another task's output file, and never edit a script a running chain is executing, because overlapping landings sweep each other's patches.
because: Two landings overlapped when a queue read a stale exit line, and one commit swept in another lane's patch before its gate; an in-place edit of a running landing script derailed it after its commit; the scripts now hold a lock.

claim: When an agent stops processes on a shared machine, stop only process ids it recorded when it started them, never by name, command-line pattern, window title or parent, because a pattern also matches the processes of every other session.
because: One stop by command-line pattern matched a path every shell wrapper carried and killed about 25 wrappers and 2 node processes of other lanes; after the rule every lane recorded and stopped its own ids.

claim: When a cleanup removes worktrees or folders on a file system with directory junctions, list and unlink every junction inside them first, then check the main tree's ignored dependency folders and the next package's size, because removal follows a junction into its target.
because: A cleanup of 28 closed worktrees followed junctions and emptied a licensed 1 GB dependency in the main checkout, invisible to the shell's link search; the next package staged 56 MB less and shipped without it until the dependency was fetched again.

claim: Read a difficulty ladder through a model of a person's hand on the input device the player really uses (reaction, misses, lapses, cursor lag and landing error per profile), one profile per level, and quote every win rate with the hand and the seed count it was read through.
because: A hockey ladder read through keys only gave pro 60 % and all-star 30 %; the same levels with the cursor through the hand gave 85 % and 10 %; a perfect hand overstated the player by 15 to 30 points at every level. The profiles were reasoning, not measured on a person.

claim: Before a scripted match goes into a gate with a win-or-lose verdict, count how many of 20 seeds it passes; a verdict that holds on fewer than all is a coin, and is replaced by the strongest line that does hold on every seed.
because: Two gate tests judged on seed 1 passed 10 of 20 and 19 of 20 seeds; one asked for three goals after the rules had gained periods. The replacement, a perfect hand beats the easiest level, held 20 of 20.

claim: A check that lives on a pre-merge list a person must remember is moved into the gate as a step with found and completed counts the night it first catches something.
because: A games-in-one-world-hash-as-alone check sat on a pre-merge list; a kernel fault introduced at 03:31 was caught by it only at 05:39 when the list was first run, and as a gate step it failed on the fault put back and named the game with both hashes.

claim: A helper that asks the physics world a question takes the space of the object that asks, never the default space of the viewport, and has a test that runs it inside a composed world.
because: A what-is-under-the-feet query asked the viewport's physics space; games composed into one world each have their own space, so the query found nothing there and a game diverged from tick 681, ending at 6,722 ticks where it ends at 1,591 alone.

claim: Carry a possessed ball or puck where the carrier's tool is drawn, measured from the rig per frame, and then re-read every rule that used the old carry point: reach, poke, boards, the zone behind the net, the goal volume.
because: A puck carried 0.95 m ahead lay under the figure in 9 of 19 stills; the rig's blade measured 3.0 m out, not the assumed 1.9; moving the carry there made it visible in 5 of 6 stills and exposed three stalls (held outside the boards, out of reach behind the net, lying inside a net without scoring).

claim: When a perfect-input bot does worse than a degraded one, look at the bot's decision policy before the level: an instant hand executes a bad habit more often.
because: A perfect hand won 13 % against the hardest level and a sharp human-like hand 30 % over 40 seeds: the bot shot whenever lined up within 40 m, the perfect hand took 93 shots against 47, and each long miss became a counter-attack; a 16 m shooting range made the perfect hand an upper bound again.

claim: Score by where the ball is each tick while play is live, not only by the event of entering the goal volume, and decide own goals and carried-in goals in the rule.
because: A puck carried into a net and released there never scored because the trigger counted entries of a loose puck; nothing moved for 10,000 frames until a time limit ended the match as a draw (1 of 120 ladder runs).

claim: A brief states that the builder's measurement outranks the brief, and the director accepts a refused acceptance line when the refusal comes with the figure and a substitute proof.
because: In one night builders refused three lines of the director's briefs with measurements: a hash that could not stay unchanged (proved by a copy without the one declaration), a 1.9 m blade that measured 3.0 m, and a 10-point tolerance at 20 seeds that needs about 100.
